title: Opening Plenary: The Geopolitics of Industrial Policy
panelists: The Rt Hon Lord Hague of Richmond; Dr Monica Gorman
description: [Draft – needs approval] Lord Hague will be in conversation with Dr Monica Gorman on the shifting relationship between geopolitics, industrial policy, and the future of industry. Lord Hague will reflect on how strategic competition, technological change, national security, and economic resilience are reshaping the choices facing governments and firms. Dr Gorman will bring a complementary perspective from her recent White House work on manufacturing policy, supply chain resilience, and sectoral competitiveness, engaging Lord Hague on what these changes mean for industrial strategy on both sides of the Atlantic. The session will connect high-level statecraft with the practical realities of industry, offering an Oxford-based conversation on the policy, political, and geopolitical forces transforming contemporary industrial systems.

title: Plenary: Value Chains and Industrial Innovation Policy
Public Policy and the Digital Stack
panelists: Diane Coyle; Annabelle Gawer; Helena Malikova
description: Online platforms have become essential infrastructures of modern capitalisms. In recent years, a few hyperscalers have shifted from consumer- to enterprise-oriented services, and from asset-light service providers to asset-heavy orchestrators of a multilayered digital stack. As digital technologies transform legacy manufacturing industries, this evolution is reshaping entire production systems. Unsurprisingly, the digital stack has become a central feature of international political and economic conflict. It has also risen to the top of national agendas for economic security, sovereignty, resilience and competitiveness. But how did we get there? And what does it portend? Are the two countries that own their own digital stacks set to dominate the global political economy? Can mid-sized economies with real technological capabilities become countervailing forces? Can these middle-powers leverage existing specializations in complex manufacturing industries to build innovation in critical areas of technology to protect their interests and remain relevant in the global arena? And can they do so without compromising existing commitments to fair employment and environmental sustainability?

title: Space: Can the Final Frontier Become a Market?
panelists: Dr Paul Bate; Rob Desborough; Nigel Chandler; Raja Roy
description: Space has become one of the most strategically significant industries of this century. Once the preserve of government agencies pursuing scientific, military and exploratory missions, it now underpins communications, Earth observation, climate monitoring, and national security. Yet a central question remains open: can space become a genuine market, or will its structure, demand and economics remain largely shaped by the state? What makes space unusual is that markets here often have to be built before demand is visible. Governments, investors, and firms must make long-term commitments under extreme uncertainty, and the commercial landscape is shaped as much by public procurement, industrial policy, and venture capital as by ordinary consumer demand. Bringing together speakers from venture capital, the space and defence industry, the UK Space Agency, and academia, this panel asks how space markets are created, financed, and governed. In doing so, we address a broader question of how markets are constructed when demand, technology, and industry boundaries are all still being formed?

title: Drug Shortages: Drivers, Consequences, and Solutions
panelists: Dr Markus Felgenhauer; Damien Holly; Mujaheed Shaikh
description: Drug shortages have hit record highs worldwide. In addition to causes common to all global industries (e.g., national disasters and geopolitical disruptions), in the pharmaceutical industry there is also a mix of manufacturing fragility, market economics, regulatory friction, and supply chain opacity. The consequences of drug shortages ripple from clinical care to public trust. This panel brings together research, policy, and industry perspectives to unpack the drivers of shortages, public policy responses, and private sector solutions. Discussion will draw on firsthand experience managing drug supply, covering the underlying economics, such as rewarding manufacturers for staying in markets with razor-thin margins, a tendency for single sources of supply, and environmental regulation continuing to push production toward Asia. Expect insights from work with data and decision-makers across several countries, and a live demo of predictive tools that flag shortage risk before it hits the shelf.

title: Infrastructure - From Concrete to Cloud: A Laggard Leviathan or a Leading Light?
panelists: Alison Baptiste CBE CEng FICE; Jim Hall FREng FRS; Julia Pyke CBE; Chetan Kotur FREng
description: Delivering large-scale infrastructure is fundamental towards realizing our future societal ambitions and meeting our global grand challenges. On the one hand, age-old challenges still exist - uneven skilled labour availability, operational complexity, and time-cost-quality pressures amidst ever increasing geopolitical turmoil and economic turbulence. On the other hand, we see remarkable advancements in machine learning, robotics & physical AI, nuclear fission & fusion, renewables, to name only a few, that are allowing us to reimagine the possible. In this panel, we will explore what this duality spells for the future of infrastructure. Will we continue to genuflect to age-old problems that continue to seemingly spring anew or will these novel breakthroughs allow us to inflect to a new reality? The answers do not just have implications for those leading, studying, or enacting large-scale projects and policy around infrastructure but also for those seeking to use these assets as springboards for new imaginative futures.

title: What Is Industry Studies Research?
panelists: Juliane Reinecke; Laura Dupin; Saurabh Bansal
description: Industry studies sits at the intersection of strategy, organization theory, operations, innovation, and public policy, yet its distinctive contribution remains a topic of debate. This panel brings together leading scholars—Sourabh Bansal, John Gray, and Juliane Reinecke—to examine what defines industry studies research, the questions it is uniquely positioned to answer, and its relevance for contemporary challenges. The discussion will explore industries as critical levels of analysis, the role of industry context in shaping organizational outcomes, and the value of integrating multiple theoretical and methodological traditions. Panellists will reflect on the field's past development, current boundaries, and future opportunities, offering insights for both established and emerging scholars interested in understanding industries as complex systems of competition, collaboration, and change.

title: Resilience and Reconfiguration of Global Supply Chains
description: As geopolitical tensions, technological disruption, and systemic vulnerabilities reshape global supply chains, new approaches to resilience are emerging. This panel examines four critical themes: (1) managing cascade risks in increasingly interconnected supply networks; (2) the growing use of supply chains as instruments of statecraft through export controls, technology restrictions, and resource access; (3) industrial resilience and supply chain reconfiguration driven by breakthrough technologies and new organisational models; and (4) the opportunities and risks created by agentic AI systems, including new approaches to visibility, coordination, and risk management. Together, the discussion explores how firms, industries, and governments can adapt to an increasingly uncertain global environment.
